1:
Why Paul asserts his apostleship to strangers is answered two ways. Gill makes it partly defensive, since false teachers insinuated that he was no apostle, and partly a claim to authority. Robertson denies the defensive motive: Paul describes himself because he is unknown to the Colossians, not because of any attack such as lay behind the opening of Galatians. Calvin argues on Robertson's ground: because the Colossians had never seen him his private name was not sufficient, so he premises that he is an apostle set apart by the will of God, from which it follows that he did not act rashly in writing to persons not known to him, since he was discharging an embassy God had entrusted to him. Henry turns the clause devotional: an apostle is a prime-minister in the kingdom of Christ, immediately called and extraordinarily qualified, and Paul attributes the office not to his own merit or sufficiency but to the free grace and good-will of God, holding himself engaged to do his utmost because he was made one by that will.

Why Timothy is named divides them. Henry finds another instance of humility, and marks that though Paul elsewhere calls him his son he here calls him his brother, an example to elder and more eminent ministers to look upon the younger as their brethren. Ellicott makes it a mark of the letter's character: the salutation is almost verbally coincident with the opening of the epistle to the Ephesians except at this point, and the naming here against the omission there marks the difference between a special letter, in which Timothy would be joined with Paul as usual, and a general letter to the churches of Asia, where the Apostle alone could rightly speak. Robertson makes it simply a function of where Paul was at the time. On the titles given the readers Henry says that towards God they must be saints, sanctified by his grace, and towards one another brethren, and in both faithful; Calvin, that the term applied to them is the more honourable, by which Paul allures them the more willingly to listen.

The two who describe the city do not agree even on its name. Barnes prefers one spelling on the authority of many manuscripts, Clarke another; both place it in Phrygia on the Lycus, which Clarke says enters the earth near the town and runs underground about three-quarters of a mile before emerging. Barnes traces its fortunes through the ancient authors, a great city to one, well inhabited to another, but by a later geographer reckoned among the smaller towns; and records that in the latter part of Nero's reign, not long after this epistle was written, Colosse and two neighbouring cities were overwhelmed together by an earthquake, from which it recovered so far that the Byzantine writers count it among the most opulent, though the town is now extinct. Clarke traces the rulers instead, from the Macedonians through the Persians and Seleucids to the Romans, and notes the government had been democratic, its first magistrate bearing a double title.

Chrysostom alone asks when the letter was written. He observes that some advantage belongs to the epistles Paul sent after he was in bonds, and places this one after the letter to the Romans, which was written before he had seen them where this was after, near the close of his preaching. His evidence is Onesimus: in the letter to Philemon Paul calls himself the aged and makes request for him, whereas here he sends the man himself, calling him faithful and beloved and a brother; and Paul could here say boldly that the gospel had been preached in all creation under heaven, which required that it had been preached a long time. He puts the letter to Timothy later still, written when Paul was at the very end of his life, and the letter to the Philippians earlier.
2:
What makes a saint is answered at opposite lengths. Gill denies three things first: they are holy not by birth, since all are unclean by nature, nor by baptism, which neither takes away sin nor gives grace, nor merely by an outward reformation; but by separation in eternal election, by imputation, Christ being made sanctification to them, and by the sanctifying grace of the Spirit in regeneration. Clarke disposes of the word in five: those who professed Christianity. Wesley divides the two titles between the two relations, the first expressing union with God, the second union with fellow Christians; Gill takes the third for true and sincere believers, constant and persevering.

The name of the town is uncertain, and both who notice it say so. Clarke reports that many excellent manuscripts, versions and fathers give a different spelling from the received one, and judges that most probably the true reading; he adds from an early historian that the city perished by an earthquake a short time after the date of this epistle, and names the village supposed to occupy the site. Robertson says only that the spelling is uncertain, the manuscripts differing between title and text, and describes the valley, whose tributary streams carried a calcareous deposit of a peculiar kind that choked them and made arches and fantastic grottoes, yet left much fertility and two prosperous cities near by. He quotes another that this was the least important church to which any of Paul's epistles were addressed, and answers that Paul had no greater message for any church than the one he gives here concerning the Person of Christ. Barnes turns aside to the letter from Laodicea which Paul bids them read, notes that the obvious sense is a lost letter of his own to that church, and that much difficulty has therefore been felt.

Whether the salutation named Christ is a textual question that divides them. Ellicott holds that the best manuscripts give simply from God the Father, varying from Paul's otherwise universal phraseology, and that such a variation can hardly be accidental; he asks whether it sprang from the Apostle's desire in this epistle to emphasize the true Godhead of Christ, an instinctive reluctance to use any phrase that might seem to distinguish his nature from the Godhead, and points to the later verse where Christ is called the mystery of God, even the Father. Robertson accepts the shorter text and notes it is the only opening benediction where the name of Jesus Christ is not joined with God our Father. Clarke reports the omission from many manuscripts, versions and fathers, and that an editor left the clause out, but judges the evidence insufficient.

Why the letter opens with thanks rather than compliment is Calvin's question. He observes that Paul makes use of thanksgiving in place of congratulation, teaching us that in all our joys we must call to remembrance the goodness of God, since everything pleasant to us is a kindness conferred by him, and admonishing us by his example to acknowledge with gratitude not merely what the Lord confers upon us but what he confers upon others. He adds that in praising their faith and love Paul both encourages them to constancy and procures their friendly regards, and that in thanking God for both he acknowledges both to be his gifts, since otherwise the gratitude were pretended. Henry lays down the rule more broadly, that thanksgiving ought to be part of every prayer, and whatever is the matter of our rejoicing ought to be the matter of our thanksgiving; and finds encouragement in the address, that we look to God as Christ's Father and our Father. Robertson notes that the word rendered always stands amphibolously between the two verbs and may be taken with either; Wesley, that there is a near resemblance between this epistle and those to the Ephesians and the Philippians.
4:
That Paul heard of their faith raises a question Barnes answers at once: it does not prove he had never been at Colosse or did not plant the church, since he uses a similar expression of the Ephesians, whose founder he undoubtedly was. Clarke turns the same parallel the other way, holding the Apostle thought the two churches in nearly the same state, the epistles being very similar in doctrine and phraseology. Robertson says the report came from Epaphras. Gill takes the faith commended to be not only assent to the doctrine but the grace of faith itself, which had not Moses nor any mere man but Christ for its object; and Calvin says the phrase is used that we may bear in mind that Christ is the proper object of faith, while love to all the saints is named not to exclude others but because, as any one is joined to us in God, we ought to embrace him the more closely.

What hope is doing here they read differently. Ellicott insists the words mean on account of the hope, so that faith and love are not merely leading up to hope but actually kindled by it, and calls the place assigned to hope here notable. Robertson leaves the connection open, thinking it likelier that the phrase attaches to the love just before, and observes that hope is here objective, the goal ahead. Barnes takes hope for the thing hoped for and makes the faith and love the evidence that such a hope was theirs. Calvin argues from the other end, that the hope of eternal life is never so inactive as not to produce love, since the man persuaded that a treasure of life is laid up for him will aspire thither and look down upon this world; and he warns that those who pervert the passage to extol the merits of works reason futilely.

On the spread of the gospel Clarke turns it into a figure, the doctrine a traveller whose object is to visit the whole habitable earth, who commenced his journey in Judea and is so rapid that he has already gone nearly through the countries under Roman dominion. Robertson calls the phrase a legitimate hyperbole, since the gospel was spreading all over the empire. Ellicott says the received text is certainly incorrect, gives the probable reading, and draws two lessons, the universality of the gospel, contrasted with all local and national religions and with the secret doctrines of speculation, and the test of its reality by practical fruit. Gill marks the free grace, that they did not seek the gospel but it came to them. Calvin guards the point: faith does not depend on the gospel's success, and though the whole world should fail and heaven should fall the conscience of a pious man must not waver.

Who Epaphras was divides them twice. Barnes makes him a minister of the church there, probably sent to consult Paul, but denies evidence that he was its founder; Ellicott makes him apparently a native of the city and its first evangelist; Clarke reports the opinion that he first preached the gospel there. On the name Clarke reports that some think him the same as Epaphroditus, and notes that one version actually reads the longer name here; Ellicott allows the shortening but calls the identification most unlikely. Robertson settles a smaller point, that the true reading is on our behalf and not on yours, so that Epaphras was Paul's messenger to Colosse. On the love reported, Barnes and Ellicott agree it was wrought by the Holy Spirit and not mere natural affection, especially love towards Paul; Gill distinguishes it from a carnal and worldly love, and Calvin says such love has an internal root, where carnal friendships depend on external causes. Wesley glosses their knowing the grace of God in truth as a true experience of its power.
9:
Why Paul prays so hard for people already doing well is answered first. Chrysostom draws the figure that as in the games we cheer on most those who are near upon gaining the victory, so Paul most exhorts those who have achieved the greater part. He marks the prudence of it: the Apostle nowhere says they are destitute of everything, but that they are deficient, the words that they may be filled hinting that they had not yet arrived. Barnes says their progress was itself an encouragement to pray and a reason for seeking higher blessings, since we are always stimulated to pray for those doing well; Calvin, that the more conspicuous the grace of God in any, the more we ought to esteem them; Henry, that having heard they were good Paul prayed they might be better.

What sort of knowledge is asked for is where the controversy first shows. Ellicott presses that it is knowledge of God's will, not speculation as to the nature of God, nor as to emanations from Deity, nor as to the reasons of his mysterious counsels; and takes the word for a full knowledge, attained in measure here and perfected in heaven. Robertson makes the word the keynote of Paul's reply to the conceit of a false wisdom, and says the cure for such intellectual upstarts is not ignorance and not obscurantism but more knowledge of the will of God; understanding, he adds, is the faculty of deciding in particular cases where wisdom gives the general principles. Henry insists that the knowledge of our duty is the best knowledge, that a mere empty notion of the greatest truths is insignificant, and that we must know God's will in order to do it. Clarke wants fullness and nothing less, as the sun fills the world with light and heat; Wesley confines it to the revealed will.

The walk that follows turns on a rare word. Ellicott says it is not found elsewhere in the New Testament but means a general disposition to please, a constant preference of the will of others before our own, safe only towards God, since otherwise it bears the bad sense it usually has. Robertson says the same, and quotes another that the end of all knowledge is conduct. Calvin makes the point at length, that this is the end for which we make proficiency in God's school, and whoever does not direct his endeavours to it may toil much yet do nothing better than wander in endless windings. Gill puts it shortly, that knowledge without practice avails nothing; and Clarke warns that even a good work may be marred by being done improperly, out of season, or in a temper of mind that grieves the Holy Spirit.

Why the prayer turns from knowledge to strength Calvin answers: it puts them in mind of their own weakness, since they will not be strong otherwise than by the Lord's help, and magnifies grace, so far is any man from standing by his own strength that the power of God shows itself illustriously in helping our infirmity. Barnes finds in the spirit with which Christians bear trials a power plainly not of human origin. Ellicott renders the phrase the strength of his glory, glory being God's manifestation of himself in love to man, and contrasts the parallel prayer in the epistle to the Ephesians, which looks to knowledge of the love of Christ where this looks to endurance. Robertson distinguishes the two graces, the one remaining under difficulties without succumbing, the other the long endurance that does not retaliate. Gill says believers are weak in themselves; Clarke makes the joyfulness a continual testimony that they please God; and Wesley calls it the highest point, not only to know and do and suffer the whole will of God but to suffer it to the end, not barely with patience but with thankful joy.
12:
That the great doctrine comes in as a thanksgiving rather than a sermon is Henry's observation, and he notices the order. Paul does not discourse of redemption in its natural order, for then he would speak of the purchase first and the application after; here he inverts it, because in our sense and feeling of it the application goes before the purchase, since we first find the benefits in our hearts and are then led by those streams to the fountain-head. Barnes makes the thanksgiving itself another mode of walking worthy, and holds that Father here means not God as Father of his creatures but the Father as distinguished from the Son, who translates us into the kingdom of the Son. Ellicott calls it the thankfulness of humility, sensible that from the Father's love we have received all and can but receive.

Why Christ is now set out at such length Calvin and Robertson answer alike and separately. Calvin says this was the only remedy for fortifying the Colossians against the snares of the false apostles, to understand accurately what Christ was, since Christ alone makes all other things suddenly vanish; there is nothing Satan so much endeavours as to bring on mists obscuring him, knowing that by this the way is opened for every kind of falsehood, so that the only means of retaining and restoring pure doctrine is to place Christ before the view such as he is. Robertson marks the same transition and calls what follows a full and final answer to the depreciation of Jesus Christ by speculative philosophy, and to all modern efforts after a reduced picture of him.

The words for fitness and inheritance are worked over closely. Clarke renders the first qualified, notes that some witnesses read called instead and that one codex has both, and takes the second for a plain allusion to the division of the promised land by lot, the lot belonging to a tribe and the portion to each family in it. Ellicott finds the same verb used of making men able ministers of the new covenant and refers it to God's foreknowledge and call. Robertson explains the noun from the pebble or piece of wood first used in casting lots and then the allotted portion, and quotes another for the sense that the share is situated in the kingdom of light. Wesley says God made us meet for glory by justifying and sanctifying us.

On the deliverance Ellicott is most exact: the verb is rescued, properly used of dragging a person out of battle or the jaws of danger; the power of darkness is a usurped tyranny and not a true kingdom; and the second verb is used of transplanting races and settling them in a new home, so that salvation, begun by rescue, is completed by settlement. Barnes gives the same sense from a historian. Wesley compresses the contrast into a line, that power detains reluctant captives where a kingdom cherishes willing subjects. Gill and Calvin both note that one of the Jewish names for Satan is darkness, and Calvin concludes that the whole world, with all its pretended wisdom and righteousness, is nothing but darkness in the sight of God. On the redemption itself Clarke reports that the clause naming the blood is omitted by most witnesses of weight and judges the reading probably not genuine, adding at once that the Scriptures declare no other way of redemption than the sacrifice of Christ; Barnes takes the verse to prove that forgiveness comes through that blood while denying it proves that forgiveness is all we obtain by it. Robertson explains the word as a release on payment of a ransom, and Calvin says the two nouns stand together without a conjunction by way of explanation, so that redemption simply is the forgiveness of sins; Wesley makes forgiveness the beginning of redemption as the resurrection is its completion.
15:
What the word image carries is the first question. Barnes says it denotes a copy which accurately and fully represents its object, against a rough sketch, and takes the verse as meeting some erroneous opinion then prevailing in those churches. Ellicott lays down two things: that the word is used in the New Testament for real and essential embodiment as distinguished from mere likeness, which he proves from four other places; and that although Paul elsewhere calls man the image and glory of God, the allusion there is to a passage saying with stricter accuracy that man was made after the image of God. Robertson calls Jesus the very stamp of the Father, both before the Incarnation and now, and sets the passage beside the openings of the fourth Gospel and of the epistle to the Hebrews. Clarke argues from the epithet: if this is the image of the invisible God, nothing that appeared in the Son could be that image, for what could be visible in the Son could be visible in the Father also.

In what sense God is invisible Gill sets out by degrees: not to the Son who lay in his bosom, nor in some sense to the angels who behold his face, but to men; not seen corporeally, though intellectually with an enlightened understanding; not in his essence, which is infinite and incomprehensible, but in his works of creation, providence and grace; and not immediately but through Christ, nor perfectly until the saints see him face to face. Wesley divides it by the two natures, the Son being in his divine nature the invisible image and in his human the visible image of the Father; Henry says the same, that Christ in his human nature is the visible discovery of the invisible God.

Here the commentators fall out. Chrysostom presses the title: whose image will you have him be, and if God's, then he is exactly like the one to whom you assign him; and he asks why no angel is anywhere called image or son while man is called both, answering that the exaltedness of the angelic nature might have thrust many into impiety, whereas man's mean and low nature is a pledge of security against it, so that where the meanness is great Scripture boldly asserts the honour, and where the nature is higher it forbears. Calvin rejects this whole method. He knows how the ancients explained the verse, since having a contest with the Arians they insisted on the equality of the Son with the Father and on his consubstantiality, while making no mention of the chief point, in what manner the Father makes himself known to us in Christ; and as for laying the whole stress of the defence on the term, by contending that a creature cannot be called the image of the Creator, he calls that excessively weak, and set aside by Paul's own use of the word for man.

What firstborn of every creature means they answer without dividing. Clarke takes it for the same thing as the name given him above every name, so that he is as man at the head of all creation, and denies that he can with any propriety be considered a creature, having himself created all things and existed before anything was made. Wesley reads it as begotten before every creature, subsisting before all worlds and from all eternity; Henry, that he was begotten before any creature was made, which is the Scripture way of representing eternity. Robertson adds that the word is no longer purely Biblical, being found in inscriptions and papyri, and denies that its use bears the conclusion Arius drew from it. Wesley alone says why the passage stands here, that by describing the glory of Christ and his pre-eminence over the highest angels the Apostle lays a foundation for the reproof of all worshippers of angels.
16:
Whether the creation meant is the new creation is settled first, against it. Gill gives three reasons: whenever the new creation is spoken of the word new is used, which is not the case here; all things in heaven are said to be created, and the heavenly bodies are not capable subjects of a new creation; and to restrain the heavenly things to angels will not do either, since those who kept not their first estate find no place there, while the good angels, having never sinned, need no renovation. Barnes denies it on his own ground, that Paul does not say Christ created all things in the spiritual kingdom, or arranged the gospel dispensation, but that everything was created by him; and observes that, as if the most comprehensive terms were not enough, the Apostle goes into a specification, as if to prevent the possibility of mistake.

Clarke reduces the two verses to four claims: that Christ is the Creator of all things visible and invisible; that whatsoever was created was created for himself, he being the sole end of his own work; that he was prior to all beings in either world; and that he is the preserver and governor of all, since by him all things consist. Allowing the Apostle to have understood his own terms, he concludes, he must have held Christ truly and properly God. Ellicott makes the same point from the prepositions, observing that Paul takes up a phrase belonging only to Godhead and usually applied to the Father and distinctly applies it to Christ, with the significant change of from whom into in whom. Wesley marks that the repeated pronoun signifies his supreme majesty and excludes every creature.

Against whom all this is aimed they name plainly. Cyril turns the verse into a creed and silences three parties: every heresy which brings in different creators of the world; those who say that the sun is the Christ, since he is the sun's Creator and not the sun we see; and those who say that the world is the workmanship of angels and so wish to steal away the dignity of the Only-begotten. Christ reigns, he adds, not by having seized another's spoils, but over his own workmanship. Robertson calls the passage a complete denial of the same philosophy in its later form, the doctrine that matter is evil and the work of a remote aeon being thus swept away. Ellicott adds that the sustaining power can even less than the creative be supposed a derivative and finite thing.

Whether the priority claimed is of dignity or existence divides them briefly. Barnes reports that those who take the creation for a moral one read the word as pre-eminence and not pre-existence, and answers that its fair meaning is priority in the order of existence, equivalent to saying that he is eternal. Ellicott says both words are emphatic, that he and he only is while all else is created, and that it is impossible not to refer to the I am of eternal existence, so the word means pre-existence, not dignity. Wesley presses the tense, that it is not said he was but he is; Gill allows both senses together. On the sustaining Robertson says Christ is the controlling and unifying force in nature, and that the permanence of the universe rests on him far more than on gravity; Ellicott glosses it as holding together in unity, obeying the primeval law of their being; Wesley says all things are compacted in him into one system, so that he is the cement as well as the support of the universe, and asks whether he is less than the supreme God. Calvin subjects the angels to Christ on four grounds: they were created by him, their creation has relation to him as its end, he existed always prior to it, and he sustains them by his power.
18:
What headship means Calvin settles against a rival sense: Paul uses the metaphor elsewhere for the vital energy diffused from a root, but here speaks chiefly of government, showing that Christ alone has authority to govern the Church, and that on him alone its unity depends. Wesley will have both, head of influence and of government. Robertson takes the church here in the general sense, not of a local body, and sets the realm of nature before against the realm of grace after. Gill says the church meant is the whole election of grace, one body whose members are neither more nor fewer.

In what sense he is firstborn from the dead they qualify. Barnes denies any literal priority, since Christ himself raised Lazarus and saints arose at his crucifixion, and makes the word mean pre-eminence among them all. Clarke makes him the first that ever resumed natural life with all its functions, never to lose it again, and notes that where the preceding verses spoke of the divine nature the Apostle now speaks of the human. Ellicott reports that an early father read here a kindred word, the first-fruits, a gloss but an instructive one, since it shows the reference is to Christ as being in his humanity the first principle of the new life to us. Wesley takes the beginning absolutely, for the Eternal, and asks who can sound this depth.

Who is the subject of the next verb is a real difficulty, the word Father being absent from the Greek. Barnes supplies it from the earlier verse where the Father is thanked for exalting the Son; Clarke reports the alternative rendering, that in him it seemed right that all fullness should dwell. Ellicott calls the construction doubtful, observes that Christ is the easier supply grammatically but accords ill with the reference of all things to the Father's good pleasure, and judges it simplest to take the fullness itself for the subject. Robertson quotes another that the fullness is a recognised technical term for the totality of the divine powers, and adds that where a later philosophy distributed those powers among aeons Paul gathers them all up in Christ. Calvin makes it a fullness of righteousness, wisdom, power and every blessing, and draws the rule that we must seek from it everything good we desire, since God communicates his gifts only by his Son; Wesley adds that it dwells in him constantly, as in a temple, always ready for our approach.

How far the reconciliation reaches marks for Ellicott the difference from the parallel epistle, which is fuller on the unity of Jew and Gentile, while this teaches something deeper, including not merely all humanity but all things in earth and heaven. Robertson says the double compound verb occurs only here, in a later verse and in that parallel, the addition marking a complete reconciliation, the phrase for the universe being used as though it were somehow out of harmony. Wesley limits the heavenly side to the saints who died before Christ came, the earthly being mentioned first because there the enmity began. Barnes guards the timing, that the death did not actually effect peace but laid the foundation of it; Clarke guards the direction: the enmity was on the creature's part, since God, though angry with the wicked every day, is never unwilling to be reconciled. Cyril states the dilemma that made the cross necessary: we were enemies through sin and God had appointed the sinner to die, so either God in his truth must destroy all men or in his loving-kindness cancel the sentence; but his wisdom preserved both, and he who died for us was no literal sheep, nor a mere man, nor an angel, but God made man. Calvin adds that we cannot be joined to God otherwise than through Christ, and that what is ascribed to him here belongs peculiarly to him.
21:
Where the alienation was seated they agree. Barnes says it was not merely by wicked works but alienation seated in the mind and leading to them, a deliberate and purposed enmity, not the result of passion but taking hold of the intellectual powers. Ellicott says they were not naturally aliens but estranged, and that the enmity of heart is not caused by wicked works but shown in them, and probably intensified by reflex action through them. Wesley says alienation of affection makes habitual enmity, the wicked works continually feeding it. Clarke turns to the word itself: where the Jews were at least by profession dedicated to God, these were given up to others, the compound signifying to be wholly the property of another. Chrysostom presses hardest, that Paul adds the clause lest we hear of the power of darkness and think it necessity; for it is not the same thing to deliver him who through necessity came to suffer and him who of his own will endures, the one worthy to be pitied and the other hated; and yet these, who not against their wills but with their wills and wishes sprang away from him and are unworthy of it, he has reconciled.

Calvin notices the turn from doctrine to persons, the general teaching being applied particularly to them so that they may feel themselves guilty of great ingratitude if they are drawn away from Christ to new inventions; and he says the arrangement must be observed, since the particular application of a doctrine affects the mind more powerfully, they being themselves a mirror of the grace offered to mankind.

Why Paul writes the body of his flesh rather than his body is asked by three. Ellicott says the meaning is his natural body as distinguished from his mystic body named above, but that this is no sufficient reason for the phrase, since no confusion was possible here; so without ascribing a distinctly polemical intention he supposes there was present to the Apostle's mind the philosophy which depreciated the body as evil and inclined to the idea that Christ had not come in the flesh. Robertson says plainly that Paul combines the two words to assert the actual humanity of Jesus against an incipient denial of it. Calvin calls the expression in appearance absurd and takes it for the human body the Son of God had in common with us, since he took this vile earthly body that he might be our Mediator and our brother and by dying become a sacrifice; and he adds that the entire blessing of redemption consists mainly in remission of sins and spiritual regeneration. Wesley distinguishes it from his body the church and makes it his entire manhood, dividing the presentation three ways, holy toward God, spotless in ourselves, unreprovable to our neighbour; Clarke divides it likewise, adding that the tree being good the fruit is good also.

What the condition threatens comes last. Gill answers that the virtue of Christ's blood does not depend on their faith or their abiding in it, but that faith and continuance are the necessary means of their presentation, so the verse shows the necessity of final perseverance. Barnes puts it without qualification: it will be impossible to be saved unless we continue to lead lives becoming the gospel. Ellicott softens the particle instead: it conveys a supposition hardly hypothetical, if as I presume, if as I trust, since the Apostle cannot refrain from warning yet refuses to anticipate failure; Robertson reads the grammar the same way, a condition assumed fulfilled with a touch of eagerness, the saint pictured as a building on a foundation and as one seated firmly in a chair. On the last clause Barnes denies that every creature can literally have heard and takes it of the design, while Clarke calls it a Hebraism for the whole human race and its two grand divisions.
24:
What it means to fill up what is behind of the afflictions of Christ is the crux, and no two agree. Barnes takes it for what Paul lacked of coming up to Christ's sufferings in the same cause. Clarke reads it of his own course, that he had still afflictions to pass through before his race of glory should be finished, and traces the imprisonment to his assertion of Gentile privilege. Wesley makes it what remains to be suffered by Christ's members, and explains why such sufferings bear his name: the suffering of any member is the suffering of the whole, and of the head especially, and they are borne for his sake; and he guards it at once, that they are necessary not to reconcile the church to God or satisfy for sin, which Christ did perfectly, but for example, for the perfecting of the saints and the increasing of their reward. Henry says the sufferings of Head and members make up as it were one body of sufferings, but that Christ suffered for the redemption of the church while we suffer on other accounts, since we do but slightly taste the cup of which he first drank deeply.

Robertson works from the word, a rare double compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, meaning to fill up in turn: it is now Paul's turn, he says, borrowing a figure from the field, Christ having had his turn, the grandest of all, and yet not having caused suffering to cease, so that there is plenty left for each of us in his time. Ellicott notes that the true text has no relative pronoun, so the sentence starts with emphatic abruptness, the same rejoicing being declared in all three epistles of the captivity. Calvin gives the purpose of the whole: Paul provides against his apostleship being detracted from by his bonds, since Satan perversely turns such things into occasions of rendering the servants of God contemptible, and he encourages them by his own example.

In what sense he is minister of the Church is marked closely. Ellicott observes that a little before he called himself a minister of the gospel and here of the Church, whereas elsewhere he is always minister of God and of Christ, the Church being named here as the Body of Christ, indissolubly united with him. Calvin sharpens the distinction with a phrase from an early father, that Paul is a servant not to the price of redemption but to the preaching of it; the Apostles serve God and Christ for the glory of both, and serve the Church to promote salvation, so the two ministries differ in reason though neither can subsist without the other. Robertson calls it God's stewardship.

What it is to fulfil the word of God they answer against the obvious sense: Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all take it for fully preaching rather than accomplishing a prediction, Clarke noting that the common meaning would give the accomplishing of God's purpose as foretold. Robertson calls it a fine phrase for a God-called preacher, to give full scope to the word of God, the preacher being an expert on that word by profession. Why the gospel is called a mystery comes last. Gill says the term marks off the gospel from the Scriptures at large, and that it is so called because it contains things which even when revealed remain mysteries to a natural man, their manner being past accounting for even by the enlightened. Barnes makes it the doctrine that salvation was to be proclaimed to all mankind, concealed for generations and therefore called a hidden truth. Chrysostom raises it higher, that before us no one knew it, neither angels nor principalities nor any created power but the Son only, and that Paul says not simply that it was hid but quite hid, since from the beginning God willed these things.
27:
Why God made the secret known at all is answered by pointing away from men. Calvin puts a bridle on presumption: they are not to inquire beyond what they ought, but to rest satisfied that it has so pleased God, whose good pleasure ought to be perfectly sufficient for us as a reason; and this is chiefly for the commending of grace, since mankind furnished no occasion for God making them participants of the secret, it being Paul's custom to set the good pleasure of God against all human merits. Gill denies four grounds in the men themselves: not their works, nor any preparation towards the gospel, of which there is naturally none, nor a foresight of their better improvement of it, nor any holiness in them, which they came by afterwards. Ellicott calls the willing emphatic, of God's own pleasure and inscrutable to man; and Robertson calls the inclusion of the Gentiles the crowning wonder to Paul, who feels the high honour keenly and meets the responsibility humbly.

What the mystery amounts to Clarke draws out as the sum and substance of the Apostle's preaching: he preached Christ as the only Saviour of sinners, and proclaimed this Christ as being in them, since the design of the gospel is to put men in possession of the Spirit and power of Christ, to make them partakers of the divine nature and prepare them for an eternal union with himself. Wesley reduces it to a phrase, Christ dwelling and reigning in them, which is the ground of their hope; and Ellicott compares the fuller definition given in the parallel epistle, where the mystery is that the Gentiles should be fellow-heirs and of the same body.

Which of the two comes first, warning or teaching, they answer three different ways. Ellicott says that in warning is implied the reproof of folly or sin, and that teaching is simply the instruction of those already warned. Wesley reverses the order outright: we teach the ignorant, and admonish them that are already taught. Robertson divides them by subject rather than sequence, warning being about practice and teaching about doctrine. Barnes takes issue with the English word itself, since warn commonly means to caution against danger, whereas the Greek means to put in mind, to admonish, to exhort, so that the Apostle's business was to bring the offers of the gospel fairly before the mind of every man.

Why every man is repeated so insistently both Robertson and Ellicott refer to the same quarrel. Robertson notes that the phrase stands three times over, in opposition to a doctrine of intellectual exclusiveness. Ellicott suggests that the word rendered perfect may carry the sense it bears elsewhere of one initiated in a mystery, so that against the exclusive claim of perfection made by the speculators in mystic knowledge the Apostle would present every man, learned or ignorant, perfect before God; and in this universality of privilege, he says, lies the glorious distinction of the gospel. Calvin makes the passage serve the authority of the doctrine, since Paul applies to his own preaching all he has declared about the adorable secret of God, having noted a little before that Christ is the sum of it, so that they might know nothing can be taught that has more of perfection than Christ. On the labour of the last verse Barnes says the word is agonizing, that Paul taxed all his energies as the wrestlers strove for the mastery in the Grecian games, and yet not by his own strength but by the power which God alone can give; and Gill says the end of it was that in the great day of account he might bring a large number and set them before Christ as the seals of his ministry.
